sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

arguments.content:
# Surfing Pelican 🐦‍⬛🌊

An animated, non-interactive 3D scene built with [three.js](https://threejs.org/) and plain ES modules.

## What you'll see

A stylized low-poly pelican carving lazy S-turns across an endlessly rolling
ocean, wings out for balance, pouch jiggling in the wind, with a spray of water
trailing off the tail of its surfboard. Clouds drift by, gulls circle overhead,
and the camera slowly orbits the action.

## How it's built

| File          | Purpose                                                                  |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `index.html`  | Entry point, loads `main.js` as an ES module.                            |
| `main.js`     | Scene, camera, sky dome, sun, clouds, gulls, and the animation loop.     |
| `waves.js`    | Shared analytic wave function (height + slopes) so water, board and spray all agree. |
| `ocean.js`    | CPU-displaced low-poly ocean mesh with foam vertex colors on the crests. |
| `pelican.js`  | The pelican + surfboard, assembled entirely from primitive geometries.  |
| `spray.js`    | Pooled water-spray particle system behind the board.                     |

Everything is generated in code — no textures or models are loaded, so the page
runs fully offline.

## Run it

```bash
npm install
npx serve .        # or any static file server
```

Or bundle it with esbuild:

```bash
esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=bundle.js
```

content.text:
Done! I built an animated surfing pelican scene with three.js. The esbuild bundle check passes (`esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` → ✅ 1.1 MB).

## What I built

**`index.html`** — entry point loading `main.js` as an ES module, with a minimal title overlay.

**`main.js`** — scene setup and animation loop:
- Gradient sky dome (custom shader), sun disc with glow, drifting low-poly clouds, and 5 gulls circling overhead with flapping triangle wings
- A slowly orbiting camera that always tracks the pelican
- The pelican carves lazy S-turns across the water, smoothly rotating its heading to follow its path

**`waves.js`** — shared analytic wave function (height + slopes) so the ocean mesh, surfboard, and spray particles all agree on where the water surface is.

**`ocean.js`** — flat-shaded low-poly ocean, CPU-displaced every frame from the wave function, with foam-white vertex colors on wave crests (with noise so it isn't a clean band).

**`pelican.js`** — the bird and its surfboard, assembled entirely from primitives (spheres, cones, boxes): crouched body, S-neck, long orange beak with a wobbling throat pouch, flapping wings with dark tips, feet planted on a red-and-cream surfboard with a skeg. The rider bobs, tilts with the wave slope, and the pouch jiggles.

**`spray.js`** — a pooled particle system (canvas-generated round sprites) shooting water spray off the board's tail with gravity, spawned at the wave surface height.

Everything is generated in code — no textures or models loaded, so it runs fully offline in the sandboxed iframe.
